implementation_notes: Scala's collections are the splitter: flatMap applies a collection-valued function to every element and concatenates the results, grouped(size) yields fixed-size chunks and sliding(size) yields overlapping windows, which the 2.13 collection documentation lists as the subdivision operators - exactly the split role. Iterating lazily (iterator/View) keeps the split streaming instead of building intermediate collections, and correlation plus sequence numbers are added by the mapping function because no framework supplies them.
pitfalls: grouped and sliding return Iterators of sub-collections, not single elements - publishing them directly sends batches.
Iterators are single-use: a stored iterator that was traversed once yields nothing afterwards; use a View to re-traverse.
flatMap over an unbounded LazyList never terminates unless the send loop is bounded.

variants.name: Akka Streams mapConcat operator
variants.implementation_notes: In a stream-based service the split is an operator: mapConcat transforms each element into zero or more elements that are passed downstream individually, and returning an empty Iterable emits nothing rather than cancelling the stream; back-pressure is part of the Reactive Streams semantics, so the splitter produces parts only when downstream demands them. Use it for real stream processing with bounded buffers; the collections form is simpler for finite in-memory composites.
variants.code_sketch:
Source(order.items)
  .mapConcat(item => List(Part(order.id, item)))   // zero-or-more per element
  .runForeach(bus.publish)
pitfalls: The mapping function must return an Iterable; a lazily recomputed Iterable re-evaluates on every demand, so return a concrete List.
Back-pressure only holds inside the stream: a blocking publish inside runForeach still stalls the materialised stream.
mapConcat is stateless - use statefulMapConcat when the split needs a running sequence counter.
